idiom_name: Dictionary<TKey, Func<T>> registry configured by a static Factory(Action<IBuilder>) method
implementation_notes: Func<TResult> delegates are the builders and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> (or ConcurrentDictionary) is the table, so no class hierarchy is needed: a static Factory(Action<IBuilder> configure) fills a dictionary and returns a closure that resolves the key and invokes the builder - the same collapse of the builder/factory interface pair that the Java edition of the catalog shows with Supplier. What replaces the classic structure is exactly this delegate-plus-dictionary pair; a concrete factory class per product is only justified when construction must be compile-time checked. Framework alternative: with Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection (.NET 8+) keyed factories are registered through AddKeyedTransient<TService>(serviceKey, implementationFactory) and resolved with GetRequiredKeyedService<TService>(serviceKey) - prefer the container when the products have their own lifetimes and dependency graph, and keep the hand-rolled dictionary when the table itself is the artifact and must stay plain data.
pitfalls: The dictionary is captured by the returned closure; configuring it while other threads create from it races, so fill it completely before publishing or use ConcurrentDictionary.
A missing key throws KeyNotFoundException at create time and nothing in the type system prevents it; assert in a test that every advertised key resolves.
The closure keeps the dictionary and every captured dependency alive for as long as the factory is referenced - a static kit is a process-wide singleton with the usual test-isolation problem.
